newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dollar rebounds,Eurobourses climb on US data.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dollar rebounds,Eurobourses climb on US data.

text.p: The dollar paused for breath on Thursday after rebounding by four yen as worries evaporated over a Washington-Tokyo trade row, while European bourses made solid gains lifted by a strong Wall Street opening.
The U.S. currency clawed back recent hefty losses in early trade after a senior Japanese official eased market fears over trade tension with the United States. It fell back slightly in mid-afternoon.

In equities, European bourses were boosted by U.S. figures showing subdued inflationary pressures. Paris was given an extra lift as anxiety faded over possible disruption to the timetable for the launch of Europe's single currency.

Most of the day's focus was on currency markets, where Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, dubbed "Mr. Yen" for his influence on exchange rates, galvanized trading with overnight comments about currencies and the trade balance.

The dollar, which plunged to a seven-month low against the yen on Wednesday, recovered after Sakakibara, director general of the Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said that Japan would act "decisively" against excessive currency moves.

He added that the issue of U.S.-Japan trade relations was "being played up excessively" and that Japan's current account surpluses would not be a major topic of discussion when leaders of the big industrial nations meet next week in Denver.

Fears that the burgeoning Japanese surplus would renew trade friction with Washington made the dollar slump to 110.70 yen on Wednesday. After Sakakibara's comments, the dollar surged to 114.20 yen before steadying at 113.98.

"There seems to be a bit of froth building up given the size of the move, but it is quite clear that the Japanese don't want the dollar to go down any further," said Henry Wilkes, the head of trading at Bank Julius Baer.
Concern about a trade row grew after U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Wednesday Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth.
"The U.S. and Japan are trying to firefight before it gets unmanageable," said Paul Meggyesi at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The U.S. currency also climbed against the mark as hopes hopes grew that EU countries would soon agree on the budget deficit stability pact which imposes fiscal discipline after they join economic and monetary union.

Expectations have increased that France, which earlier asked for time to consider the issue, would soon agree to the pact. European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Thursday he believed a deal would be reached at the EU summit in Amsterdam next week.

"The easing of the problems vis-a-vis the stability pact has seen people move out of marks," said White at Yamaichi. The dollar is seen as a safe-haven currency in the event of a "soft " European single currency.

The growing EMU optimism, coupled with yet another trading peak on Wall Street at Thursday's opening, also boosted the Paris bourse, which suffered steep losses after the socialist victory in this month's election.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index climbed two percent to 2,755.6 points before falling back slightly in mid-afternoon.
"This rise is a little surprising with the Socialists in power but the market seems to not be taking this into account while it waits for the first policy measures," one trader said.

The U.S. data, which showed weaker-than-expected retail sales, allayed fears of a near-term interest rate rise and sent the Dow Jones industrials climbing up by nearly one percent to 7643.21 points--and boosted European stocks.
In Frankfurt, where floor trading ended well up even before Wall Street opened, dealings on the computerised IBIS index surged 1.6 percent, lifted by Wall Street and the revitalised dollar.
"The dollar is strong today and the retail figures in the U.S. were encouraging," a German share trader said.
But, unlike Paris, Frankfurt still had reservations about prospects for monetary union and these were seen limiting further advances.
Of central importance was the dispute between Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer over revaluation of assets.
The Bundesbank shot down an original proposal to use the revaluation proceeds to help Germany meet criteria goals in the Maastricht Treaty.
"Everyone is intrigued as to what is going to happen," one trader said.
London, Europe's biggest bourse, perked up after Wall Street's opening after a dull showing in the morning to register gains of 0.7 percent. CURRENCIES AT 1430GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.7226 marks and 113.98 yen compared with 1.7144 marks and 111.36 yen in late trade on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1430 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 31.9 points at 4,756.7.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 56.52 points at 2,752.71.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index ended up 30.56 points at at 3,707.99. The computerised IBIS index was up 65.0 points at 3736.87.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed in the afternoon at $342.20 an ounce, compared with Wednesday's close of $344.05. Silver was down two cents at $4.75.
